questions.stem: According to the fundamental Law of Demand, what happens to the quantity demanded of a normal good when its price increases (ceteris paribus)?

options.option_text: The quantity demanded of the good increases.
The quantity demanded of the good decreases.
The quantity demanded remains absolutely constant.
The supply of the good immediately drops to zero.

questions.explanation: The Law of Demand states that there is an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded. As price rises, consumers demand less of the good, assuming all other factors remain constant (ceteris paribus).

questions.stem: In a competitive free market, the 'equilibrium price' is exactly defined as the specific price at which:

options.option_text: The government strictly artificially fixes the maximum retail price.
The producers make the highest possible gross financial profit.
The quantity demanded perfectly equals the quantity supplied.
The consumers can easily buy unlimited quantities of the good.

questions.explanation: Equilibrium price (or market-clearing price) is the price where the demand curve and supply curve intersect. At this point, the exact amount consumers wish to buy equals the amount producers wish to sell.

questions.stem: Tea and coffee are substitute goods. If the price of tea suddenly rises sharply, what will happen to the demand curve for coffee?

options.option_text: It will shift to the left (decrease in demand).
It will remain totally unchanged and unaffected.
It will become a perfectly vertical straight line.
It will shift to the right (increase in demand).

questions.explanation: Because tea and coffee are substitutes, an increase in the price of tea makes it relatively more expensive. Consumers will switch from tea to coffee, increasing the demand for coffee at every price level (a rightward shift of the demand curve).

questions.stem: Which of the following factors would cause a 'movement along' the supply curve, rather than a 'shift' of the entire supply curve?

options.option_text: A change in the selling price of the good itself.
A sudden improvement in manufacturing technology.
An increase in the cost of necessary raw materials.
A heavy government tax imposed on the producers.

questions.explanation: A change in the good's own price causes a change in 'quantity supplied' (a movement ALONG the curve). Changes in technology, input costs, or taxes alter the willingness to supply at ANY price, causing a SHIFT of the entire curve.

questions.stem: What does a perfectly inelastic demand curve look like when plotted on a standard graph (Price on Y-axis, Quantity on X-axis)?

options.option_text: A straight horizontal line parallel to the X-axis.
A steep line curving smoothly downward to the right.
A straight vertical line parallel to the Y-axis.
A straight line sloping upwards at exactly 45 degrees.

questions.explanation: Perfectly inelastic demand means consumers will buy exactly the same quantity regardless of how high or low the price goes (Elasticity = 0). Since quantity (X-axis) never changes, the curve is a vertical line.

questions.stem: A 'Giffen good' is a rare economic concept that actively violates the standard Law of Demand. Which of the following is the defining characteristic of a Giffen good?

options.option_text: It is a highly luxurious status symbol whose demand strictly increases because wealthy people want to show off.
It is an inferior good whose demand increases when its price increases, due to a dominant negative income effect.
It is a perfectly substitute good whose demand drops to absolute zero when its price increases even slightly.
It is an essential lifesaving medical drug whose demand remains absolutely perfectly constant regardless of price.

questions.explanation: A Giffen good is an extreme type of inferior good. When its price rises, the consumer's real income falls so drastically that they must cut back on more expensive foods and buy EVEN MORE of the basic Giffen staple (e.g., cheap bread or potatoes) to survive. Option B describes a Veblen good.

questions.stem: If the government imposes a binding 'price ceiling' (maximum legal price) below the natural market equilibrium price, what will be the immediate economic result?

options.option_text: A market surplus, because quantity supplied will significantly exceed quantity demanded.
A new equilibrium, where demand automatically safely shrinks to meet the lower supply.
An immediate increase in overall product quality to strictly justify the lower price.
A market shortage, because quantity demanded will significantly exceed quantity supplied.

questions.explanation: A price ceiling set below equilibrium forces the price down artificially. At this low price, consumers demand more, but producers are willing to supply less. This mismatch creates a shortage (e.g., rent control leading to housing shortages).

questions.stem: Petrol and cars are widely treated as complementary goods. If the government slashes fuel taxes causing petrol prices to fall sharply, what is the most likely direct effect on the automobile demand market?

options.option_text: Demand for cars falls due to the income effect on consumers
Demand for cars rises, shifting the demand curve rightward
Supply of cars increases as manufacturers anticipate profits
The car market remains unaffected since car prices did not change

questions.explanation: B is correct because petrol and cars are complements — cheaper petrol lowers the total cost of motoring, making car ownership more attractive and shifting car demand rightward. Option C is the most tempting distractor but confuses demand-side and supply-side responses; it is consumers, not producers, who react first to a complementary good's price change.

questions.stem: As rural incomes rise due to MGNREGA wage hikes, demand for coarse jowar (sorghum) in those households is observed to fall. This classifies jowar as which type of good?

options.option_text: A Giffen good, since both income and demand move in opposite directions
A normal good with inelastic demand responding only to price changes
An inferior good, since demand falls as consumer income rises steadily
A Veblen good, whose demand rises with social status of the consumer

questions.explanation: C is correct: an inferior good is defined by a negative income elasticity of demand — as income rises, consumers switch to preferred substitutes, reducing demand for the inferior good. Option A is the classic trap: Giffen goods are a special sub-case of inferior goods, but their defining feature is that demand rises when the good's own price rises — income direction alone does not establish 'Giffen' status.

questions.stem: The cross-price elasticity of demand between good X and good Y is calculated as −1.5. Which interpretation of this value is most accurate in standard demand theory?

options.option_text: X and Y are complements; a 1% rise in Y's price reduces demand for X by 1.5%
X and Y are substitutes; a 1% rise in Y's price raises demand for X by 1.5%
X is an inferior good; a 1% income rise reduces demand for X by 1.5%
X and Y are independent goods with a weak inverse price relationship

questions.explanation: A is correct: cross-price elasticity (∂Qx/∂Py × Py/Qx) is negative for complementary goods because the goods are consumed together — a rise in Y's price reduces its quantity demanded, which drags down demand for its complement X. Option B describes substitutes, for which cross-price elasticity is positive. Option C confuses cross-price elasticity with income elasticity of demand — a completely different measure.

questions.stem: An excise duty is imposed on cigarettes, a good with highly inelastic demand. Compared to a similar tax on a good with elastic demand, which outcome best describes the tax burden on cigarette buyers?

options.option_text: Buyers bear a smaller share of the tax due to habit-driven consumption patterns
Buyers bear a larger share of the tax because they cannot easily reduce consumption
The tax burden falls equally on buyers and sellers regardless of demand elasticity
Sellers absorb the entire tax as buyers switch instantly to substitutes in the market

questions.explanation: B is correct: when demand is inelastic, consumers have few substitutes and cannot significantly reduce consumption in response to a price rise, so sellers can pass most of the tax forward as higher prices. The more inelastic the demand, the greater the share borne by buyers. Option A inverts the logic — inelastic demand means buyers are less able to escape the tax, not more. Option D applies to perfectly elastic demand, not inelastic.

questions.stem: Ernst Engel, the 19th-century German statistician, formulated a landmark empirical regularity about household expenditure. Which statement correctly encapsulates Engel's Law?

options.option_text: Richer households consistently spend a higher share of income on food
Food expenditure grows proportionally with income across all income groups
Higher income leads to a fall in the absolute money spent on food per month
As income rises, the share of income spent on food falls steadily over time

questions.explanation: D is correct: Engel's Law states that as household income increases, the proportion (budget share) spent on food declines, even though the absolute rupee amount spent on food may actually increase. This reflects food's characteristic as a necessity with income elasticity below 1. Option C is the most dangerous distractor — it confuses the falling share with a fall in absolute spending, which is not what Engel observed.

questions.stem: The Cobweb Theorem models cyclical price fluctuations in agricultural markets due to lagged supply responses. Under which structural condition will prices converge to equilibrium over successive periods?

options.option_text: Supply elasticity exceeds demand elasticity at the current equilibrium price point
Both demand and supply have identical price elasticities at the equilibrium point
Demand elasticity exceeds supply elasticity at the current equilibrium price point
Supply response is instantaneous with no lag in producer adjustment to prices

questions.explanation: C is correct: in the Cobweb model, convergence (stability) requires the supply curve to be steeper than the demand curve at equilibrium, which geometrically corresponds to supply being less price-elastic than demand. When demand elasticity > supply elasticity, each price oscillation is smaller than the last and the market homes in on equilibrium. Option A describes the opposite — a more elastic supply relative to demand produces an explosive (divergent) cobweb where oscillations grow without bound.

questions.stem: A binding Minimum Support Price (MSP) for rice is set ₹200 per quintal above the free-market equilibrium. Which combination of welfare effects does standard economic analysis predict in this scenario?

options.option_text: Producer surplus rises, consumer surplus falls, and a deadweight welfare loss emerges
Both producer and consumer surplus rise as the price floor boosts total market value
Consumer surplus rises as rice availability increases under the guaranteed MSP
Producer surplus falls as unsold grain accumulates beyond the MSP intervention level

questions.explanation: A is correct: a binding price floor above equilibrium forces consumers to pay a higher price, shrinking consumer surplus. Producers who successfully sell receive a higher price, expanding their surplus — but because quantity traded falls below the competitive level, mutually beneficial trades are blocked and a deadweight loss (triangle) emerges. Option B is wrong because total surplus cannot rise with a price floor; the DWL represents value destroyed. Option C is the classic exam trap — the MSP benefits sellers, not buyers, who face higher prices and buy less.
